sections.b: Half of the book of Joshua is maps. God tells the aged Joshua that much land remains, yet orders him to allot it anyway (Joshua 13:1–7). The tribes east of the Jordan have their shares from Moses; the rest are given by lot, first at Gilgal to Judah and Joseph, then at Shiloh to the other seven after a written survey (Joshua 14–19). Judah's south border copies Moses' south border for the whole land (Joshua 15:1–4; Numbers 34:3–5). The lists admit what was not taken: Jerusalem, Gezer, the valley cities, Dan's coastal land (Joshua 15:63; 16:10; 17:12; 19:47). Yet the section closes, "So the LORD gave Israel the whole land he had sworn to give their ancestors" (Joshua 21:43).

Joshua holds two claims side by side: every good word came true (Joshua 21:45; 23:14), and nations remain who will be driven out only if Israel stays loyal (Joshua 23:4–13). Traditional readers take the first as fulfillment in principle and the second as the task left to Israel. Critical readers see two views of the conquest combined by the Deuteronomistic writer. Hebrews 4:8 reads the gap theologically: Joshua's rest was not the final one.

common: The land was the gift of God, received rather than earned (Joshua 24:13).
uncommon: Some critical scholars hold that the town lists of Joshua 15–19 reflect Judah's and Israel's royal administration centuries after Joshua.

sections.b: Joshua 13–19 gives each tribe its land: Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh east of the Jordan; Judah in the south; Joseph's two tribes in the central hills; Benjamin between them; Simeon inside Judah; Zebulun, Issachar, Asher and Naphtali in Galilee; Dan on the coastal plain until it moves north. Levi receives towns in all the others instead of land, so with Joseph counted twice there are still twelve shares (Joshua 14:3–4). Simeon's absorption into Judah fulfills Jacob's words about Simeon and Levi (Genesis 49:7).
sections.refs: Joshua 13:8–33; Joshua 14:1–5; Joshua 15:1–12; Joshua 16:1–4; Joshua 18:11; Joshua 19:1–48; Genesis 49:5–7

sections.h: East and west of the Jordan
sections.b: Joshua 22 tests whether the Jordan divides Israel. The eastern tribes build an altar "as a witness" that they too have a share in the LORD, and the western tribes, after nearly going to war, accept it (Joshua 22:10–34). The episode affirms one Israel on both banks.

At 85, Caleb reminds Joshua of Moses' oath at Kadesh and asks for the hill country of Hebron, where the Anakim lived: "Perhaps the LORD will be with me, and I will drive them out" (Joshua 14:12). Three times the chapter says he "followed the LORD fully" (Joshua 14:8, 9, 14). He drives out the three sons of Anak, offers his daughter Achsah to the man who takes Debir, and gives her the upper and lower pools when she asks (Joshua 15:13–19). Hebron's town later became a priests' town, while its fields stayed with Caleb (Joshua 21:11–12).

sections.h: Caleb and Joshua frame the land
sections.b: L. Daniel Hawk and other commentators note that the land division is bracketed by the two faithful spies. Caleb receives first, choosing the hardest land (Joshua 14:6–15); Joshua receives last, choosing a small town (Joshua 19:49–50). The frame suggests that those who trusted God at Kadesh are the ones who now hold the land, and that the leader takes his share last.

Joshua names Og as "one of the last of the Rephaim" (Joshua 13:12) and the Rephaim's land as forest in the hills (Joshua 17:15). Hebron was Kiriath-arba, after Arba "the greatest man among the Anakim" (Joshua 14:15; 15:13). Caleb drives out Sheshai, Ahiman and Talmai, the very sons of Anak the spies had feared (Joshua 15:14; Numbers 13:22). The Valley of Rephaim lies on Judah's border by Jerusalem (Joshua 15:8).
sections.refs: Joshua 13:12; Joshua 14:12–15; Joshua 15:8; Joshua 15:13–14; Joshua 17:15; Numbers 13:22

sections.b: Joshua 20 carries out the law of Numbers 35 and Deuteronomy 19. A killer who acted "by mistake, without meaning to" may run to a city, state his case to the elders at the gate, and live there until he stands trial and the high priest dies (Joshua 20:3–6). Israel sets apart Kedesh in Galilee, Shechem and Hebron west of the Jordan, and Bezer, Ramoth-gilead and Golan east of it (Joshua 20:7–8). The protection covers the foreigner too (Joshua 20:9). All six are also Levite towns (Joshua 21:13, 21, 27, 32, 38). The Greek text of Joshua 20 is shorter and lacks most of the wording drawn from Deuteronomy, which many scholars take as a sign the Hebrew was expanded.
sections.refs: Joshua 20:1–9; Joshua 21:13; Joshua 21:21; Joshua 21:27; Joshua 21:32; Joshua 21:38; Numbers 35:9–34; Deuteronomy 19:1–13

uncommon: Some scholars think the cities of refuge were an ideal that was never fully put into practice, since no biblical story shows anyone fleeing to one.

sections.b: Joshua says three times what Levi received instead of land: the LORD's offerings by fire (Joshua 13:14), the LORD himself (Joshua 13:33), and the priesthood (Joshua 18:7). Joshua 21 lists the forty-eight towns with pastureland: thirteen for Aaron's priests in Judah, Simeon and Benjamin, near the later temple; ten for the other Kohathites; thirteen for the Gershonites; twelve for the Merarites. 1 Chronicles 6:54–81 repeats the list with many small differences. Scholars date the list anywhere from Joshua's time to after the exile.
sections.refs: Joshua 13:14; Joshua 13:33; Joshua 14:3–4; Joshua 18:7; Joshua 21:1–42; 1 Chronicles 6:54–81; Numbers 35:1–8

sections.b: The second half of the book shows Joshua as an old man dividing the land (Joshua 13:1), granting Caleb's request (Joshua 14:13), answering Joseph's complaint by telling them to clear the forest (Joshua 17:14–18), and urging the slow tribes, "How long will you hang back?" (Joshua 18:3). He receives his own town last, Timnath-serah (Joshua 19:49–50). He gives two farewells: a warning to the leaders (Joshua 23) and a covenant at Shechem where he says, "I and my family will serve the LORD" (Joshua 24:15). He dies at 110 and is called, at last, "the servant of the LORD" (Joshua 24:29).
sections.refs: Joshua 13:1; Joshua 17:14–18; Joshua 18:3; Joshua 19:49–50; Joshua 23:1–16; Joshua 24:15; Joshua 24:29–30; Judges 2:8–9

sections.b: When the eastern tribes build an altar by the Jordan, Israel sends Phinehas with ten leaders before going to war. He recalls Peor, where his own zeal stopped the plague (Joshua 22:17; Numbers 25), and Achan's sin. When he hears the tribes' explanation, he declares, "This day has shown us that the LORD is among us" (Joshua 22:31). The zealous priest becomes the one who prevents a civil war. The book ends with Eleazar buried on "the hill of his son Phinehas" (Joshua 24:33).

Shechem is a city of refuge and a Levite town (Joshua 20:7; 21:21), and the place where Joshua gathers all Israel for his last covenant (Joshua 24:1–28). There he calls the people to put away foreign gods, as Jacob had done at the same oak (Genesis 35:2–4), and sets up a great stone "beneath the oak at the LORD's sanctuary" (Joshua 24:26). Joseph's bones are buried in Jacob's field there (Joshua 24:32). The Greek text moves the covenant to Shiloh (Joshua 24:1, 25), probably a later change.
sections.refs: Joshua 17:2; Joshua 20:7; Joshua 21:21; Joshua 24:1–32; Genesis 33:18–20; Genesis 35:2–4

sections.b: Joshua 24 is the Bible's fullest covenant renewal outside the Torah. It opens "This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says," reviews God's acts from Terah to the conquest, demands that Israel serve the LORD alone, calls the people as witnesses against themselves, records the words in a book, and sets up a stone witness (Joshua 24:2–27). Scholars since George Mendenhall have compared this pattern with Hittite treaties. Joshua's warning, "You cannot serve the LORD," and the people's reply, "We will serve the LORD," make loyalty a free and serious choice (Joshua 24:19–24).

Joshua's farewell warns, "Suppose you break the covenant" (Joshua 23:16), using avar, "cross over," the book's word for crossing the Jordan. The covenant is pictured as a boundary not to be crossed. Holding on (dabaq) to the LORD (Joshua 23:8) is set against holding on to the nations (Joshua 23:12).

A generation after Moses' ruling, Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah come before Eleazar, Joshua and the leaders and remind them: "The LORD commanded Moses to give us an inheritance among our relatives" (Joshua 17:4). They receive five of Manasseh's ten shares west of the Jordan (Joshua 17:5–6). The Samaria ostraca of the 700s BC name districts called Noah and Hoglah in Manasseh's hills, showing that the sisters' names stuck to the land.

sections.h: Forced labor and peoples who remained
sections.b: The land chapters admit that the ban was not carried out everywhere. Ephraim put the Canaanites of Gezer to forced labor (Joshua 16:10); Manasseh could not take the valley cities and later did the same (Joshua 17:12–13); Judah could not drive out Jerusalem's Jebusites (Joshua 15:63). Joshua's farewell treats the remaining nations as a danger to Israel's faith, not a military threat (Joshua 23:7, 12–13). Readers who struggle with the ethics of conquest point to these chapters as evidence that the sweeping language of total destruction was ancient war rhetoric, not a record of what happened.
sections.refs: Joshua 15:63; Joshua 16:10; Joshua 17:12–13; Joshua 23:7–13; Judges 1:27–35; Deuteronomy 20:10–18

sections.b: In Joshua 22 Israel gathers to make war on its own eastern tribes over an altar, following the law against an apostate town (Deuteronomy 13:12–18). An inquiry comes first, and war is avoided. Judges 20 shows what happens when it is not.

sections.h: "The LORD gave them rest all around"
sections.b: Joshua announces the fulfillment of Deuteronomy's promise of rest from enemies (Joshua 21:44; 22:4; 23:1; Deuteronomy 12:9–10). Yet the same book speaks of nations that remain (Joshua 23:4–13), and Judges shows the rest broken again and again. Hebrews 4:8 concludes that Joshua's rest was not the last word: "If Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken afterward about another day."
sections.refs: Joshua 21:44; Joshua 22:4; Joshua 23:1; Deuteronomy 12:9–10; Psalm 95:11; Hebrews 4:1–11

sections.b: In Joshua's maps Jerusalem lies on the seam between Judah and Benjamin. Judah's north border runs "along the south slope of the Jebusite city" through the Valley of Ben-hinnom (Joshua 15:8), and Benjamin's list includes "Jebus (that is, Jerusalem)" (Joshua 18:28). Neither tribe could drive out the Jebusites (Joshua 15:63; Judges 1:21). The city remained Jebusite until David took it (2 Samuel 5:6–9). The Amarna letters show it was already called Urusalim in the 1300s BC.
sections.refs: Joshua 15:8; Joshua 15:63; Joshua 18:16; Joshua 18:28; Judges 1:21; 2 Samuel 5:6–9

sections.h: Bethel, Luz and Beth-aven in Joshua
sections.b: Bethel stands on the border of Joseph and Benjamin. Joshua 16:2 runs the border "from Bethel to Luz," as if two places, while Joshua 18:13 says "Luz, that is, Bethel." Nearby lies Beth-aven, "house of wickedness" (Joshua 18:12), a name Hosea later threw at Bethel itself (Hosea 4:15). Bethel is listed among Benjamin's towns (Joshua 18:22), though Judges 1:22–26 has the house of Joseph capture it.

After the conquest, "The whole community of the Israelites came together at Shiloh, and there they set up the tent of meeting. The land had been brought under their control" (Joshua 18:1). The remaining lots are cast "before the LORD, at the entrance of the tent of meeting" (Joshua 19:51). In Joshua 22 the one lawful altar "stands in front of his tabernacle" (Joshua 22:19, 29). The phrase "brought under control" and the word "finished" (Joshua 19:51) echo creation and the building of the tabernacle (Genesis 1:28; Exodus 40:33).
sections.refs: Joshua 18:1; Joshua 19:51; Joshua 22:19; Joshua 22:29; Genesis 1:28; Exodus 40:33

sections.b: Shiloh becomes Israel's gathering place in Joshua 18. There the tent of meeting is set up, Joshua sends out surveyors and casts lots for seven tribes (Joshua 18:1–10), the Levites receive their towns (Joshua 21:2), and the tribes gather when they fear the eastern altar (Joshua 22:12). Excavations at Khirbet Seilun, led by Israel Finkelstein, found an Iron Age town destroyed around 1050 BC. The Greek text sets even the final covenant at Shiloh (Joshua 24:1, 25), though the Hebrew says Shechem.

sections.h: Witness stones and a witness altar
sections.b: Joshua ends with two memorials that speak. The eastern tribes' altar is a "copy" of the LORD's altar, built as "a witness between us and you" (Joshua 22:27–28; compare 22:34). At Shechem Joshua sets up a great stone under the oak: "Look at this stone. It will stand as a witness against us, because it heard everything the LORD said when he spoke with us" (Joshua 24:27). The Stone of Bohan son of Reuben marks a border (Joshua 15:6; 18:17). At Shechem, Ernst Sellin's excavators found a large standing stone, broken and fallen, before the temple fortress in 1926; G. Ernest Wright's team set it upright again in 1962 and linked it to Joshua 24.
sections.refs: Joshua 15:6; Joshua 22:26–28; Joshua 22:34; Joshua 24:26–27; Genesis 31:44–52; Isaiah 19:19–20

sections.b: Joshua's farewell forbids even speaking the names of the nations' gods (Joshua 23:7; Exodus 23:13). At Shechem he admits that Israel's ancestors "served other gods" beyond the Euphrates and in Egypt (Joshua 24:2, 14), and calls the people to get rid of the foreign gods "you have among you" (Joshua 24:23). The Passover Haggadah quotes the verse: "In the beginning our ancestors served idols."
sections.refs: Joshua 23:7; Joshua 23:16; Joshua 24:2; Joshua 24:14–15; Joshua 24:20–23; Genesis 35:2–4

sections.b: The house of Joseph receives the central hills, divided between Ephraim and Manasseh (Joshua 16–17). Its leaders complain that one lot is too little, and Joshua sends them to clear the forest (Joshua 17:14–18). The book ends by fulfilling Joseph's last wish: his bones, carried out of Egypt, are buried at Shechem in the field Jacob bought (Joshua 24:32; Genesis 50:25; Exodus 13:19). Hebrews 11:22 counts Joseph's instructions as an act of faith.
sections.refs: Joshua 16:1–4; Joshua 17:14–18; Joshua 24:32; Genesis 50:24–25; Exodus 13:19; Hebrews 11:22

sections.b: Martin Noth counted Joshua 23 among the key speeches by which the Deuteronomistic writer marked turning points in Israel's history, with Joshua 1, 1 Samuel 12 and 1 Kings 8. Its language is Deuteronomy's: be strong, do not turn to the right or the left, hold on to the LORD, love him; and its warning that Israel may "vanish from the good land" reads to many as written in view of the exile (Joshua 23:6–16). Joshua 22:5 and 21:43–45 carry the same voice.

The book's second half shows foreigners in several lights. Caleb, the model of faith, is a Kenizzite, from a clan with Edomite ties (Joshua 14:6). The cities of refuge protect "the foreigner living among them" (Joshua 20:9). Peoples who remained are put to forced labor (Joshua 16:10; 17:13). Joshua's farewell forbids marrying the remaining nations, because they would lead Israel to other gods (Joshua 23:12–13).

Joshua 14–21 carries out the command of Numbers 26:55–56: the land is divided by lot. The lots are cast "before the LORD" at Shiloh after a written survey (Joshua 18:6–10). Each tribe's lot "comes out" or "comes up" (Joshua 16:1; 18:11; 19:1), and even the Levites' towns are assigned by lot (Joshua 21:4–8). The Talmud says Eleazar consulted the Urim and Thummim as well, and the lot confirmed it (Bava Batra 122a).
sections.refs: Joshua 14:2; Joshua 18:6–10; Joshua 19:51; Joshua 21:4–8; Numbers 26:55–56; Numbers 33:54

sections.b: Joshua lists "all the regions of the Philistines" and their five rulers among the land still to be taken (Joshua 13:2–3). Judah's list nonetheless claims Ekron, Ashdod and Gaza to the Wadi of Egypt (Joshua 15:45–47). Dan's original land lay beside them, and its towns Timnah and Ekron appear later in Samson's story (Joshua 19:43; Judges 14:1).

Judah receives the first and fullest allotment: a border traced on all four sides and about 115 towns in districts of the Negev, the Shephelah, the hill country and the wilderness (Joshua 15:1–62). Simeon's towns lie inside it (Joshua 19:1–9). The detail reflects Judah's later importance as the kingdom that kept these records.

Joshua remembers Balaam twice. Among the Midianites killed in Moses' war, the Israelites "put Balaam son of Beor, the diviner, to the sword" (Joshua 13:22). In the covenant history God says, "I refused to listen to Balaam. Instead he blessed you over and over" (Joshua 24:10).
